sources.title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code (AI That Works, Boundary channel)
sources.note: Local faster-whisper machine transcript, no speaker labels; Dex presents, Vaibhav Gupta co-hosts. Attributed by content; the 'I never use xhigh / I use medium almost always' and BAML-guideline passages read as Vaibhav's and were not carded as Dex's. Video is not in the inventory (only the October essay is, section at line 80).

sources.title: Astra beats Opus 5.5 on SlopCodeBench, xhigh considered harmful (X article, context only)
sources.note: Read only to say where the video adds to or differs from it; not carded (another reader has it).

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Opus 5.5 median did way better than Opus 5.5x high, like three percentage points.
cards.claim: On the October SlopCodeBench run Opus 5.5 at medium effort beat Opus 5.5 at xhigh on strict pass rate; the video says about three points, whereas the article's 28 vs 25 of 196 checkpoints is about 1.5 points (a discrepancy).
cards.evidence_detail: One run per setting, 36 problems, 196 checkpoints; strict pass rate. The video gives no run-to-run variance; the article states one campaign per setting.
cards.landing: Effort routing: default Claude-family verifiers and workers to medium rather than xhigh, pending a repeat on a FixFlow task.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you use medium, it's cheaper and better for Opus. But if you use medium for Astra, it's cheaper, but not as good.
cards.claim: The effort effect is model-family specific: medium is cheaper and better for Opus, but for the OpenAI models (Astra) medium is cheaper and worse, so xhigh pays off there.
cards.evidence_detail: Same single-run-per-setting data; Dex adds the caveat that this may just be the shape of this benchmark.
cards.landing: Effort routing table keyed per model family, not one global effort setting; do not copy an OpenAI-family xhigh finding to Claude verifiers.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: And that might just be the shape of this benchmark.
cards.claim: Dex hedges his own effort finding live: the Claude-medium versus OpenAI-xhigh split may be an artefact of this benchmark, so it is not a general rule (the article says one campaign per setting cannot show variance).
cards.evidence_detail: Self-caveat; no repeat runs or variance given in the video.
cards.landing: Treat 'medium beats xhigh' as a hypothesis to test on FixFlow's own verifier tasks, not a settled routing rule.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're paying more, but you get better performance from these models when you use X high
cards.claim: For the OpenAI-family models more effort buys more strict passes at higher cost, with an overall upward cost-versus-success trend, except where a model spends heavily and does not improve.
cards.evidence_detail: Cost versus success-rate chart described on screen; exact dollar numbers not spoken (article: xhigh costs 2.11-4.22x medium in the three full pairs).
cards.landing: Cost-aware effort setting: spend xhigh only on model families where it is shown to help.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: fable 5.1 x high which was like way more expensive and not impressive at all
cards.claim: Fable 5.1 at xhigh was far more expensive and not impressive at solving the benchmark, so Dex sees it as a spec double-checker rather than a coder.
cards.evidence_detail: Chart read on screen; the article puts Fable's cost at about 8.68x GPT-6.1 Medium with three fewer strict passes.
cards.landing: Model routing: use the expensive model for verifying against a spec, not for implementation.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable is great in my opinion just for like double checking a spec
cards.claim: Dex's current use of Fable is as a checker of whether work abides by a spec, which is a verifier-role routing suggestion.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal usage opinion, no numbers.
cards.landing: Reviewer and refuter model choice: consider a spec-conformance checker role distinct from the implementer.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: basically the strict pass is basically the current checkpoints. tests and every previous test has to pass
cards.claim: Strict pass rate means the current checkpoint's tests plus every earlier checkpoint's tests all pass, and one regression locks the model out of any later strict pass, which is why Dex treats it as the metric that matters.
cards.evidence_detail: Metric definition; the video also notes a failing checkpoint caps all later strict scores.
cards.landing: Verifier design: check regression against all earlier requirements, not only the latest change.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: each challenge has three to eight checkpoints, and there's like 30 challenges with 196 checkpoints.
cards.claim: The benchmark is about 196 checkpoints across 30-36 problems (he says 30 then 36 in the same talk), each checkpoint inheriting the previous code so the model builds on its own slop.
cards.evidence_detail: Benchmark size only; one run per model-effort setting.
cards.landing: Sample-size context when weighing any effort-level claim: 196 checkpoints, one run per setting.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: only Astra was like basically like three out of, yeah, three out of six, 36.
cards.claim: Even the best run finished with failing tests: only Astra ended with all tests passing on 3 of 36 problems, so checkpoint success is not the same as a working final program.
cards.evidence_detail: Final-snapshot test run on 36 problems; transcript wording is garbled, so the exact count is uncertain.
cards.landing: Run the full suite on the final state, not only per-step checks.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you just do the lights off factory thing and just feed a model features and high-level design
cards.claim: A lights-off factory that feeds a model features and high-level design accumulates slop, so the odds of a correct answer without breaking earlier requirements fall over time.
cards.evidence_detail: Framing of the SlopCodeBench thesis; supported by the benchmark's low strict pass rates.
cards.landing: Argues for refactor and maintenance checkpoints in the phase routine rather than only feature checkpoints.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we haven't figured out how RL models on like software maintainability.
cards.claim: Models lack maintainability intuition because RL makes them good at coding but nobody has worked out how to train for maintainability, which is partly an act of disobeying the instruction.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoned opinion, no data.
cards.landing: Maintainability has to be imposed from outside (rules, linters, reviewers) because the model will not volunteer it.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: tokens it cost to produce tasks matters way less than the maintainability of the software over time
cards.claim: Dex says token cost and agent time matter far less than long-term maintainability because maintainability compounds, a position that argues against optimising for cheap runs.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated in the intro; he and the co-host agree users would pay roughly twice the tokens, even for 20% cleaner code.
cards.landing: Cost-versus-quality trade-off for effort and verifier spend: weigh maintainability gains over per-run cost.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we actually want to measure like how much garbage the models leaving your code base.
cards.claim: Dex reports that the SlopCodeBench researcher persuaded him not to exclude scratch, test and verifier files from the quality score: leftover junk is slop the benchmark should count.
cards.evidence_detail: The article gives the filter result: only Opus Medium's _work folder (45 files, 41,265 lines) was affected; slop presence dropped to 92.90%.
cards.landing: Verifier or CI check that flags leftover scratch files and stray artifacts, since a skipped cleanup is otherwise invisible.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: about two, I think it was 212 custom like slop detectors.
cards.claim: The benchmark's quality measure combines about 150 custom AST-based AI-slop linters with 50-60 standard code metrics (cyclomatic complexity, traversal depth, pass-through 'tramp' data) for about 212 detectors, with function-level hits marking every line of the function as slop.
cards.evidence_detail: Counts given from memory ('I think'); machine transcript.
cards.landing: Mechanical code-quality metrics as a verifier signal; the linter set is an example of a ready-made battery.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Opus 5.5 X high did the best on the slop metrics. It had the least like triggers.
cards.claim: Opus 5.5 xhigh had the lowest slop coverage even though Opus medium had more strict passes, so cleaner code and passing regression tests diverged and the quality metric did not predict the pass rate.
cards.evidence_detail: Article numbers: 77.75% versus 94.25% slop coverage, 25 versus 28 strict passes; he cautions the linters date from March and may miss new patterns.
cards.landing: Quality metrics and pass rates are different verifier signals; do not use one as a proxy for the other when choosing effort.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a lot of them are from March. So it's like traded. Probably need to be updated.
cards.claim: The slop linters are partly stale (many from March), so newer models may have new slop patterns they do not catch and the detector set needs regular refresh.
cards.evidence_detail: Caveat stated live; a follow-up episode with the researcher was suggested.
cards.landing: Any lint or quality battery adopted needs a refresh loop; a static set will miss newer failure patterns.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable actually had the like the almost the most functions ... and had the lowest like average complexity
cards.claim: Fable wrote nearly the most functions and had the lowest mean cyclomatic complexity, but Dex warns that smaller functions do not mean the code is not slop, so a single metric can be gamed.
cards.evidence_detail: Chart of function counts and weighted mean cyclomatic complexity; he had not read the code. Opus 5.5 wrote about 200,000 lines, Sol medium the fewest.
cards.landing: Do not gate on a single complexity metric; pair it with test pass rate and a human or reviewer read.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we're using the best possible harness for that model at that given time
cards.claim: Each model was run in its own default harness (Claude Code for Claude, Codex for GPT, OpenCode for GLM), so the comparison mixes model and harness effects.
cards.evidence_detail: Clarified after the co-host asked; he corrects 'best' to 'most aligned default'.
cards.landing: Caveat when transferring results to FixFlow: the Claude Code harness result is the relevant one for Claude effort settings.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you give the model more back pressure, then boom, you actually get to like this whole thing
cards.claim: Dex endorses baking quality metrics into the compiler or loop as back pressure (telling the agent it made the codebase worse), noting lower complexity often means fewer bugs; he calls this the missing feedback in the benchmark.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex relays this from the co-host's BAML experiment (guidelines beat baseline on most complexity metrics, but not worst-function complexity); no Dex-run numbers.
cards.landing: Back-pressure script feeding complexity and slop metrics to the agent during the work, not only at review.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'd be really interested to see the difference between a, like, here's the thing, go build it, prompt
cards.claim: Next step: Dex wants to compare plain 'build it' prompts against runs with a feedback battery or target quality score on SlopCodeBench, which he lists as a task for next week.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated intention; no results yet.
cards.landing: If run, this tests exactly whether backpressure verifiers change outcomes; worth watching.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can start measuring skills, you can measure linters, you can measure all sorts of things
cards.claim: With a benchmark plus quality metrics you can compare many variants of a skill or linter (ten rather than three) by measuring the git diff after each variant, so skills and rules can be tested rather than assumed.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated while Dex reacts to the co-host's BAML run, which re-ran the same challenge N times per prompt variant; no counts given.
cards.landing: A measurement loop for the 13 new skill packages: run each with and without the skill on a fixed task and compare metrics.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I have a whole other thing to go on about like how tests are freaking pointless now.
cards.claim: In passing Dex says that for fast zero-to-one work thrown out every few months, tests are close to pointless now, a hint of a position he does not develop here.
cards.evidence_detail: Aside, undeveloped; contrasts with his insistence on regression tests as the strict metric.
cards.landing: Nowhere obvious; FixFlow has a live ledger, so this would not apply there without more argument.

cards.source_title: Why Opus Medium Beats X-High at Writing Maintainable Code
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models are not good at centralizing, at redefining abstractions, at creating, like doing refactoring.
cards.claim: Models will refactor well when told to but do not volunteer centralising or refactoring as requirements change, so refactor steps must be explicitly asked for.
cards.evidence_detail: Thesis statement for the benchmark; backed only by the benchmark's low strict rates.
cards.landing: Add an explicit refactor or consolidation step to the phase routine instead of expecting the agent to do it unprompted.

gaps: The video gives no number of runs beyond what the article says (one campaign per model and effort setting) and nothing on run-to-run variance; the 'three percentage points' in the video is about 1.5 points by the article's 28 vs 25 of 196.
The video says '30 challenges' and later '36 problems'; unresolved in the transcript.

The 'I never use xhigh / I use medium almost always (Ben Davis said low for GPT 5.5)' remarks read as the co-host's, not Dex's, so no card; Dex does not say in this video what practitioners should set effort to.
No cost figures are spoken; the cost ratios (2.11-4.22x, $178.51, 8.68x) come only from the article.
The BAML guideline and compiler-pressure experiment (N runs per prompt, metrics improved except worst-function complexity) is the co-host's; carded only where Dex adopts the back-pressure point.
The co-host's rule of banning checked-in README and markdown files and scripts was stated as 'the same rule' in his repo; not carded as Dex's (an agent-context pollution point, which may bear on W1).
Machine transcript with no speaker labels and garbled passages (counts such as '3 of 36', 'Ben Davis', 'Armand').
